newsitem.title: USA: Leading U.S. House Democrat wants China MFN revoked.
newsitem.headline: Leading U.S. House Democrat wants China MFN revoked.

text.p: U.S. House of Representatives Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt on Tuesday called on Congress to revoke China's trading privileges but stopped short of advocating a boycott on Chinese goods.

At a news conference before a speech to the Economic Club of Detroit, Gephardt said he wanted the Chinese to "have a new understanding" of what it meant to be in a fair trading relationship with the United States and the rest of the world.

"I don't think that means a boycott," he said. "I think that means we can continue to trade but on a different basis. In other words, they would not experience the same tariff basis as other nations."

In the speech, the text of which was obtained ahead of delivery, Gephardt broke with President Bill Clinton and urged Congress to vote to overturn Clinton's decision last week to renew China's Most Favoured Nation trade status for another year. Without MFN, duties on imports from China would soar to high levels not seen since the 1930's. Only a handful of countries do not enjoy MFN status.

The Missouri Democrat, a leading contender to challenge Vice President Al Gore for his party's presidential nomination in 2000, criticised China's human rights record and trade policies, which he said include "blackmailing" companies into giving China technology and trade secrets that will make it an economic powerhouse.

At his news briefing, Gephardt said to return to MFN trading status China would have to halt the production and sale of goods made by prisoners and people in forced labour camps. He said China must improve human rights, worker rights and the standard of living of its people to compete on a level basis with other nations.
He defended his opposition to MFN for China by saying that human rights should not be separated from trading status.

"If you give normal trading status to a country that has no human rights and no worker rights, you are ensuring that you're going to be competing with a country that has a very low standard of living and no hope that that standard of living will go up," he said. That, in turn, will put pressure on U.S. wages and the standard of living of Americans.

He added that major U.S. companies may miss out on some business contracts with China but Washington must maintain leadership on the human rights issue as it did in South Affica. "I sympathise with the plight of our business community and believe that we have to become, as we were in the case of South Africa, a world leader for human rights and proper trade policy," he said.
Gephardt said he believed European countries and other major economic powers would follow the U.S. lead and China would eventually be forced to improve human rights policies.

In his speech, he accused Clinton of being "too weak" with China and said Clinton's policy of engagement to try to bring about changes in China on human rights, trade policies, nuclear technology and missile sales has not worked.
Gephardt noted that the U.S. trade deficit with China hit nearly $40 billion in 1996 and is likely to exceed $50 billion this year.
The White House responded quickly to Gephardt's remarks, saying revoking China's MFN would be like declaring "economic war" on the world's most populous country.

"The suspension of normal trade relations with China would be, in some sense, a declaration of economic war on China and would further isolate China from the world community," White House spokesman Michael McCurry said in Paris, where Clinton signed a pact between NATO and Russia on European security.

It was the second time in a week Gephardt has gone against his party's president on a major issue. Last week, he told his fellow Democrats he would vote against the balanced budget deal worked out between the White House and Republicans who control Congress. Gephardt said the budget plan would not eliminate the deficit and would be too harsh on citizens.

Many trade analysts believe congressional efforts this year to revoke China's MFN status will be unsuccessful as they have been every year since the 1989 Chinese army crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square. But with U.S. labour unions and liberal groups joining forces with conservative religious and social groups to fight China's MFN, the vote this year is expected to be closer than last year.
